profiles.presentation: {patientName}, a 50-year-old man, attends the hernia clinic for pain two years after left groin hernia repair. Lifting and squatting bring on a deep ache. He also has intermittent burning near the scar and describes a transient contour change after some lifting episodes.

node.stem: Which diagnostic procedure should be selected next for {patientName}'s pain?

answerChoices.label: Dynamic inguinal and pelvic magnetic resonance imaging
answerChoices.rationale: Persistent mechanical uncertainty after a relevant local ultrasound, together with a musculoskeletal alternative, supports selected dynamic cross-sectional evaluation rather than attributing the entire complaint to one positive maneuver.

answerChoices.label: Contrast hip magnetic resonance imaging with arthrography
answerChoices.rationale: Hip-provoked pain deserves consideration, but a hip-restricted study does not address the persistent repaired-groin uncertainty as well as the offered pelvic/groin study.

answerChoices.label: Ilioinguinal nerve block with cutaneous sensory mapping
answerChoices.rationale: A diagnostic block could help the superficial sensory complaint, but that component does not settle the deep exertional pain or intermittent contour history.

node.explanation: There are overlapping pain observations, not a single established cause. A technically relevant negative ultrasound reduces concern for a demonstrated hernia but leaves the deeper mechanical complaint unresolved. Selected dynamic cross-sectional assessment can address the repaired groin and competing pelvic causes. Neither the hip maneuver nor the superficial sensory response proves the cause of every symptom. This is not a routine MRI sequence for all postrepair pain, and no recurrent hernia is declared proved.

node.stem: Which repair should be used to continue {patientName}’s operation?

answerChoices.label: Laparoscopic transabdominal preperitoneal repair
answerChoices.rationale: The landmarks identify a prior anterior mesh repair. A posterior approach avoids repeating dissection through that scarred anterior compartment.

answerChoices.label: Open anterior Lichtenstein mesh repair
answerChoices.rationale: This repeats the anterior plane identified by the mesh and cord relationships.

answerChoices.label: Open anterior Shouldice tissue repair
answerChoices.rationale: Changing from mesh to tissue repair does not avoid the previously operated anterior compartment.

node.explanation: Mesh beneath external oblique with the cord superficial to it identifies the previous anterior compartment. Continue with a posterior preperitoneal approach rather than repeat that scarred plane. This item selects the approach during the present operation; it does not order another operation or claim TAPP is preferred over every other posterior technique.

items.value: The old mesh lies directly under the external oblique and over the inguinal floor. The spermatic cord runs superficial to it. Dense scar joins the mesh edge to the cord.

items.label: Recurrence
items.value: The recurrent bulge emerges at the medial mesh edge. The overlying tissues are intact.

answerChoices.label: Laparoscopic transabdominal preperitoneal repair
answerChoices.rationale: The landmarks identify a prior anterior mesh repair. A posterior approach avoids repeating dissection through that scarred anterior compartment.

answerChoices.label: Open anterior Lichtenstein mesh repair
answerChoices.rationale: This repeats the anterior plane identified by the mesh and cord relationships.

answerChoices.label: Open anterior Shouldice tissue repair
answerChoices.rationale: Changing from mesh to tissue repair does not avoid the previously operated anterior compartment.

node.explanation: Mesh beneath external oblique with the cord superficial to it identifies the previous anterior compartment. Continue with a posterior preperitoneal approach rather than repeat that scarred plane. This item selects the approach during the present operation; it does not order another operation or claim TAPP is preferred over every other posterior technique.
sourceLabels: Official summary of International groin hernia guidelines

audit.reason: Immediate clinic transfer is essential safety teaching, but forceful reduction and next-day antibiotics are caricatures in an overt obstructive emergency. Propose harder hospital-chart decisions; manager must retain necessary clinic-transfer onboarding coverage.
audit.historyPolicy: Preserve old definition, frozen encounters, timing/order identities and FSRS; manager decides future supply.

visibleContext.chiefComplaint: Painful groin bulge that no longer reduces
visibleContext.presentation: A 68-year-old woman with BMI 22.1 has a newly painful groin bulge that no longer reduces. Findings: Prior clinical documentation identifies an inguinal hernia, New inability to reduce a previously reducible groin bulge, Increasing groin pain, Alert mental status, and Localized tenderness.

node.stem: A previously reducible groin bulge became painful and nonreducible this morning. The patient is vomiting and increasingly distended. What should the clinic do?

answerChoices.label: Book a routine elective hernia appointment
Continue repeated forceful reduction attempts in clinic
Start outpatient antibiotics and reassess tomorrow

node.explanation: The acute loss of reducibility with pain, vomiting, and distension raises concern for obstruction or strangulation. Transfer promptly for emergency surgical-capable evaluation.
sourceLabels: Update of the international HerniaSurge guidelines for groin hernia management (BJS Open / HerniaSurge, 2023; doi:10.1093/bjsopen/zrad080)

terminalDispositions.consequenceNarrative: Acute irreducibility plus obstructive symptoms cannot safely wait for routine referral.

visibleContext.chiefComplaint: Recurring groin bulge with activity-limiting discomfort
visibleContext.presentation: A 49-year-old woman with BMI 26.0 reports a documented inguinal hernia whose recurring discomfort now limits usual lifting or exercise. Findings: Prior clinical documentation identifies an inguinal hernia, Groin bulge that increases with standing or exertion, Bulge is readily reducible on examination, Recurring discomfort now limits lifting or exercise, Stable general appearance, and Bulge becomes less apparent while supine.

node.stem: A known inguinal hernia remains soft and reducible, but increasing aching now limits routine activity. There is no vomiting, distension, skin change, or systemic illness. Choose the clinic disposition.

answerChoices.label: Refer for a nonemergency surgical consultation
Provide observation alone with no referral option

node.explanation: A reducible hernia with activity-related symptoms is appropriate for elective surgical evaluation. The absence of acute red flags makes emergency transfer unnecessary.

node.stem: Which patient fits the guideline-supported population in whom watchful waiting with return precautions may be offered?

answerChoices.label: A man with a reducible, minimally symptomatic inguinal hernia
A woman with a newly diagnosed, reducible, minimally symptomatic groin hernia
A patient with a newly painful nonreducible bulge
Any adult whose groin bulge is currently tolerable

node.explanation: Watchful waiting is a supported option for selected adult men with a reducible asymptomatic or minimally symptomatic inguinal hernia. It requires safety-netting and should not be generalized beyond that evidence base.

rankedConcepts.title: Acute irreducibility, partial-wall entrapment and bowel viability
rankedConcepts.decision: Choose reduction versus urgent operation, then assess tissue that reduced before inspection.
rankedConcepts.rawEvidence: Change from prior reducibility, focal examination, preserved passage, partial-wall geometry and enhancement.
rankedConcepts.closestCredibleError: Use stool passage or disappearance of a lump as proof of tissue viability.
rankedConcepts.errorConsequence: Delay threatened-bowel assessment or resect tissue without assessing it.
rankedConcepts.testingRelevance: High clinical consequence, clinically interpretable competing errors, distinct preoperative and intraoperative stages.
rankedConcepts.weightBasis: Qualitative editorial priority for general-surgery residents; no exam frequency, recalled questions or official test weight is asserted.
rankedConcepts.coverageAndGap: New/revised hospital-chart decisions add reduction selection and viability after spontaneous reduction; simple recovery observation is still a future gap.

round2ParkedObjectives.reason: The supported fact is the need to assess previously concerning bowel, but the available record does not fairly distinguish all real inspection approaches. Keeping only one inspection choice preserved the named-omission shortcut. No unsupported viability cutoff, mandatory resection rule or availability tie-breaker is introduced.

rankedConcepts.closestCredibleError: Treat open skin access as anterior mesh or apply the opposite-plane rule using only the most recent operation.
rankedConcepts.errorConsequence: Reenter scarred tissue without recognizing complexity or misidentify an unused compartment.
rankedConcepts.testingRelevance: Common operative planning, with plausible anatomy/access confusion; strongest gap is the unrepresented posterior-to-anterior direction.

rankedConcepts.errorConsequence: Miss a consequential compartment or defer indicated repair.

rankedConcepts.decision: Offer observation or elective assessment using function under the actual original demand and interval change.
rankedConcepts.rawEvidence: Painless lifting despite a contour, site-specific provocation, attempted usual load and response to reduction.
rankedConcepts.closestCredibleError: Equate a positive image with the cause of all pain or completed modified duty with recovery.
rankedConcepts.errorConsequence: Unnecessary operation, delayed assessment or unfulfilled expectations for separate pain.

rankedConcepts.decision: Choose a properly targeted ultrasound or cross-sectional assessment after determining what was actually acquired.
rankedConcepts.rawEvidence: Acquisition worksheets, marked site, observed event, complete cine records and proximal neck relationships.
rankedConcepts.closestCredibleError: Treat missing exports as unperformed imaging, wrong-site imaging as a negative groin examination, or MRI as a universal next step.
rankedConcepts.errorConsequence: False reassurance, redundant testing or unsupported protocol priority.

round2ParkedObjectives.reason: After the adequately targeted negative acquisition, existing guidance allows further cross-sectional assessment but does not uniquely rank all credible protocols without an additional patient-specific indication or constraint. rankedConcepts.title: Readiness for invasive chronic postoperative pain treatment
rankedConcepts.decision: Distinguish time since repair from actual exposure to a specialist pain-treatment program.
rankedConcepts.rawEvidence: Separate postoperative and treatment intervals, ongoing disability, assessed recurrence and treatment tolerance.
rankedConcepts.closestCredibleError: Select fixed mesh removal or neurectomy based only on elapsed time or a block response.
rankedConcepts.errorConsequence: Premature irreversible treatment with uncertain benefit or worsened pain.

rankedConcepts.coverageAndGap: New concept. Exact selective-versus-triple neurectomy and mesh-removal rankings remain withheld absent a patient-specific evidence basis.

question.stem: Which inguinal-hernia plan should be offered to Daniel at this review?

answerChoices.label: Repeat dynamic groin ultrasound before planning
answerChoices.rationale: The diagnosis and reduction are already established; there is no unresolved acquisition or anatomy question here.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The diagnosis and reduction are already established; there is no unresolved acquisition or anatomy question here.

answerChoices.label: Arrange elective inguinal repair now
answerChoices.rationale: Repair can be discussed, but attributing the current running limitation to this painless protrusion is unsupported. The requested plan incorporates Daniel's preference to defer.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Repair can be discussed, but attributing the current running limitation to this painless protrusion is unsupported. The requested plan incorporates Daniel's preference to defer.

answerChoices.label: Continue hernia observation with return precautions
answerChoices.rationale: A man completing usual activity without protrusion-related limitation can choose informed observation. The separate attachment pain does not automatically negate that option.

question.explanation: Daniel's limiting pain is dissociated from the protrusion during the activity actually attempted. Informed observation is a reasonable hernia policy under his stated preference, with return precautions and reassessment if the hernia changes. This does not dismiss the separate painful condition or guarantee that symptoms will remain mild.

node.currentUpdate: Daniel's scan shows a right inguinal sac that enters during strain and reduces at rest. He completes his usual warehouse lifts while the contour is visible, without groin pressure. The pain that stops running is medial to the pubis and is reproduced by resisted adduction. He prefers to defer an operation if reasonable.

manualAuditAnnotations.55: The legacy first-study item advertises ultrasound availability and compares venous/plain-film modalities. Its four finite profiles vary age without changing the keyed inference.
manualAuditAnnotations.56: The r2 imaging labels are parallel, but the same first-study rule follows an absent office lump. It is a surface variant rather than a new protocol/adequacy decision.
manualAuditAnnotations.57: Trunk-movement pain and explicit absence of imaging add symptoms without changing initial ultrasound selection. A useful replacement must interpret an acquired record rather than recite modality order.
manualAuditAnnotations.58: The r4 strain-protocol labels improve wording without changing the first-ultrasound construct. Negative office findings and muscle context do not earn a separate scored inference.
manualAuditAnnotations.59: Returned diagnosis and activity limitation appear in the update and again in the management task. Elective referral directly matches that supplied interpretation.
manualAuditAnnotations.60: The r2 task calls the hernia confirmed symptomatic and repeats the same plans. Cosmetic wording changes do not remove the supplied management conclusion.
manualAuditAnnotations.61: The key combines consultation and risk review, while individualized waiting/support choices vary in credibility and scope. Actual functional attribution is not tested.
manualAuditAnnotations.62: The r4 management labels are specific, but the update declares that same-site pain interrupts activity. The question repeats a referral rule rather than require a competing current inference.
manualAuditAnnotations.63: The r5 MRI record could distinguish a painless protrusion from attachment pain, but paired explanation/plan options create another answer dimension and an overlapping combined-pain repair choice.
manualAuditAnnotations.64: The r6 flexion/adduction comparison contains a task-specific wording match and an adduction negative that removes a distractor. A muscle-label match should not be counted as more inguinal management coverage.
manualAuditAnnotations.65: The r7 timing options contrast referral now with rehab completion and image progression after a clear reduction-responsive episode. Replace arbitrary delay policies with actual changed functional evidence.
manualAuditAnnotations.66: The legacy running variant has the same availability cue and irrelevant imaging distractors as the lifting variant. It has no accepted basic role for this exact item.
manualAuditAnnotations.67: The r2 running variant changes the setting but not the first-ultrasound rule. Parallel modality labels do not create two consequential inferences.
manualAuditAnnotations.68: The r3 adds adduction and a photograph, but explicit no-prior-imaging framing still leads directly to first ultrasound. Added symptoms do not alter the chosen stage.
manualAuditAnnotations.69: The r4 protocol wording repeats first-study selection across the running family. Retire near-duplicate supply instead of treating detail as resident difficulty.
manualAuditAnnotations.70: The adequate-negative dynamic study matters, but MRI versus sports-medicine assessment is not uniquely ranked by the broad recorded claims. A narrowed anatomical question avoids pretending to resolve every pain source.
manualAuditAnnotations.71: A team request for cross-sectional imaging supplies the stage permission that removes repeat ultrasound. Selecting strain MRI over hip MRI is then largely a protocol match.
manualAuditAnnotations.72: Two saved supine views do not establish that the examiner never acquired other regions or provocation. The replacement preserves missing-export versus actually unperformed-acquisition provenance.
manualAuditAnnotations.73: The worksheet establishes an adductor acquisition, but the task already requests ultrasound and a standing contour. A posture/modality matrix permits obvious component matching; retain the registry-only protocol identity historically.
manualAuditAnnotations.74: The original running management item supplies confirmed exercise-limiting hernia. Identical four plans and absent red flags make referral direct recall.
manualAuditAnnotations.75: This retained r10 function exhibit is nearly the passed r11 companion. Keep the exact passed version rather than adding both to fresh supply; the actual crate attempt remains consequential evidence.
manualAuditAnnotations.76: The r2 management task supplies confirmed symptomatic anatomy and repeats the same alternatives. It does not require functional attribution beyond the author's summary.
manualAuditAnnotations.77: The r3 referral key uniquely includes risk review against individualized waiting/support labels. It is an intermediate draft, not additional gap coverage.
manualAuditAnnotations.78: The r4 repeats referral for explicitly limiting same-site protrusion. Hip rehabilitation lacks the close current functional discriminator supplied by the later passed version.
manualAuditAnnotations.79: The r5 image/adduction observations may support conservative attribution, but the explanation/plan pairs overlap and combined-pain repair is ambiguous. Consolidate into the narrower observation decision.
manualAuditAnnotations.80: The r6 has tolerable work, a hernia twinge and separate running pain. The key alone matches adductor wording; keep the task-specific principle without another muscle-label match.
manualAuditAnnotations.81: Completed shifts and improved jogging do not establish tolerance of the original crate task. The r7 observation key overinterprets unqualified completion; the replacement explicitly records the original load.
manualAuditAnnotations.82: The r8 modified-duty distinction improves reasoning, but broad hernia/attachment labels were made concrete in frozen B2A07. Do not keep superseded duplicate supply.
manualAuditAnnotations.83: The r9 correctly updates MRI chronology to ultrasound and preserves the usual-load restriction, but is a historical near-duplicate of passed r11. Preserve that exact passed version and this history.
manualAuditAnnotations.84: The legacy standing-shift question has an ultrasound-availability cue and venous/plain-film foils. It repeats the same one-step first-study objective.
manualAuditAnnotations.85: The r2 standing-shift variant improves labels but keeps initial modality selection after a transient lump. It adds no acquired-evidence interpretation.
manualAuditAnnotations.86: The r3 adds a hip symptom, but the no-imaging statement still makes this first-study selection. It does not establish one assessment's priority in every mixed-pain case.
manualAuditAnnotations.87: The r4 strain-protocol wording does not interpret a prior acquisition. Its stage remains the same basic first-ultrasound rule.
manualAuditAnnotations.88: The wrong-site resting record is consequential, but excluded/established/unresolved answer pairs vary in evidence scope and caution. Use a concrete target/protocol comparison instead.
manualAuditAnnotations.89: A record containing resting views alone does not prove standing strain was never acquired. Routine MRI/resting CT foils also privilege the only explicitly dynamic option.
manualAuditAnnotations.90: The original standing-shift management item supplies confirmed activity limitation and asks for its matching plan. It duplicates the basic referral family.
manualAuditAnnotations.91: The r10 actual-work exhibit is useful, but current passed r11 adds a distinct recurrence-plane decision. Keep that passed version and avoid another redundant broad referral item.
manualAuditAnnotations.92: The r2 confirmed-symptomatic task and identical four plans repeat the referral rule. It adds no inference beyond the original.
manualAuditAnnotations.93: The r3 comprehensive key versus individualized waiting/support choices creates a scope cue. Raw site-specific function should carry attribution rather than an authored pain-limit summary.
manualAuditAnnotations.94: The r4 labels are specific but same-site activity-limiting protrusion already supplies the management interpretation. A separate hip symptom does not automatically earn another decision.
manualAuditAnnotations.95: The r5 key uniquely combines repair and hip assessment, while a distractor explicitly omits hip care. That complete-plan cue bypasses interpretation of the two pain sites.
manualAuditAnnotations.96: The r6 uniquely combined consultation/ongoing-care key and repeat MRI at another stage weaken the options. Useful interval observations should support comparable hernia policies.
manualAuditAnnotations.97: The r7 repeats referral timing against rehab completion and scan-growth delays. Continued care belongs in shared context rather than an easy key-matching referral item.
manualAuditAnnotations.98: The r8 later hip-focused limitation is a useful counterfactual but should be a focused hernia-attribution boundary, not another broad assessment-label task. The new observation scenario preserves the dissociation principle.
manualAuditAnnotations.99: The r9 referral objective is already represented by frozen newer recurrence and interval-function items. Repeat ultrasound or hip rehab is weak once reduction-responsive restriction has been shown.
manualAuditAnnotations.100: The original N1 maps a medial wall defect directly to transversalis fascia. It is recall and overlaps protected approved anatomy; replace fresh supply with a dynamic target-and-care decision.
manualAuditAnnotations.101: The teaching schematic gives medial/above-ligament position, then the task directly names its reinforcement layer. An image does not itself create a consequential second inference; the separate asset check records availability.
manualAuditAnnotations.102: The applied medial-defect idea matters, but anatomy/repair labels can imply limited operative scope without adequate support. Rebuild using moving versus static targets, actual work limitation and parallel care policies.
manualAuditAnnotations.103: The old block and new contour are useful, but naming the booked repeat nerve procedure advertises the action to delay. Replace this scaffold with actual acquisition provenance and three diagnostic investigations.
manualAuditAnnotations.104: The adequate-negative postoperative MRI draft includes a reproduced hip ache without evidence establishing priority over hip assessment or a block. It precedes the explicit owner hold and is not a resolved key.
manualAuditAnnotations.105: Preserve the exact owner decision hold. Broad MRI does not establish priority over hip radiographs or ilioinguinal block in this mixed case. Propose a separate narrowed objective without altering or clearing the held version.
manualAuditAnnotations.106: Prior mesh-plane interpretation matters, but an operation already opened anteriorly does not establish a universal immediate TAPP conversion. Rewrite as elective clinic planning and preserve the passed B2A05 version.
manualAuditAnnotations.107: Immediate clinic transfer is essential safety teaching, but forceful reduction and next-day antibiotics are caricatures in an overt obstructive emergency. Propose harder hospital-chart decisions; manager must retain necessary clinic-transfer onboarding coverage.
manualAuditAnnotations.108: The pilot supplies documented activity-limiting reducible hernia and compares referral with emergency transfer and observation alone. This is an overt disposition rule beside an implausibly incomplete option.
manualAuditAnnotations.109: The population key repeats the patient's description; women, acute irreducibility and any tolerable lump are easily rejected. It tests a demographic rule rather than a functional clinical boundary.

lastQuestion.stem: Which interpretation of Theo's injection effect and persistent pain is supported?

answerChoices.label: Cutaneous effect demonstrated; neuropathic contribution excluded
answerChoices.rationale: The side-specific sensory change supports a cutaneous effect, but one nonresponse does not exclude all overlapping neural or mixed pain mechanisms.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The side-specific sensory change supports a cutaneous effect, but one nonresponse does not exclude all overlapping neural or mixed pain mechanisms.

answerChoices.label: Cutaneous effect unestablished; neuropathic contribution excluded
answerChoices.rationale: This discards the observed side-specific sensory change and then overstates the exclusion value of persistent pain.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: This discards the observed side-specific sensory change and then overstates the exclusion value of persistent pain.

answerChoices.label: Cutaneous effect demonstrated; neuropathic contribution unresolved
answerChoices.rationale: The before/after side comparison supports a cutaneous effect. Persistent burning does not establish whether an overlapping or mixed neural mechanism contributes.

answerChoices.label: Cutaneous effect unestablished; neuropathic contribution unresolved
answerChoices.rationale: The limited mechanism conclusion is appropriate, but the observed injected-side sensory change should not be discarded just because pain persists.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The limited mechanism conclusion is appropriate, but the observed injected-side sensory change should not be discarded just because pain persists.

lastQuestion.explanation: The injected-side sensory change establishes an observed cutaneous effect, not coverage of every possible pain pathway. Persistent burning does not exclude all neuropathic or mixed contributions. Interpret delivery evidence and pain response separately within specialist assessment rather than calling a negative response either a failed delivery or a definitive exclusion.

withdrawnAuthoredAttempts.reason: Final author gate rejected both the cautious umbrella version and a balanced matrix: a single negative block cannot defensibly exclude every neuropathic contribution, so the exclusion component remained dismissible and the remaining sensory comparison was too easy. Retire the historical scored variant in favor of the component-specific response objective; preserve historical negative-block evidence as a future gap.

review.title: Marked femoral swelling: timing of repair
clarityIssues: The anatomical exhibit does not identify its modality or the examiner/report supplying these observations.

cues.phrase: pressing here does not reproduce the marked lump
cues.why: The second exhibit row explicitly dismisses the competing target instead of requiring the learner to reconcile it.

fairness: Elective repair is the defensible offered answer for this reducing, nontender femoral hernia; the record does not establish an emergency.

The intended anatomical inference fails the deletion test: a nonpregnant woman with a confirmed groin hernia still merits timely repair assessment if the marker actually corresponds to the inguinal defect. Thus distinguishing the two routes does not change the offered action.
This report is an offline editorial review of candidate-visible fields, not source verification or clinical approval. PASS entries also remain needs_clinician_review.
suggestions: Make target localization change an actual repair or investigation decision, with clinically credible alternatives and a supported patient-specific discriminator. Do not obscure the current stability findings.
Identify the source of the anatomical observations and remove a competing lesion that does not affect the decision.

review.title: Separate activity-limiting pain from an incidental inguinal protrusion
fairness: Observation with return precautions is the best offered hernia policy: actual usual lifting is tolerated despite the protrusion, while a different activity reproduces pain at the adductor attachment.

The two steps are symptom attribution using the discordant activity/site findings, then applying the selected-male observation option with the patient's preference. Elective repair is a credible temptation but is not the best response to the demonstrated limiting symptom.
The preference is legitimate decision information, not an instruction to observe regardless of findings. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.
suggestions: Preserve the distinction between the activity actually completed and the painful activity, and the explanation's limited claim about symptom attribution.

review.title: New reduction-responsive lifting limitation after observation

cues.phrase: focal inguinal pressure makes him put the load down as the lump appears
cues.why: Together with resolution on reduction, this spells out the symptomatic-hernia trigger; the offered alternatives contain no genuine unresolved competing decision.

cues.phrase: with return precautions and reassessment if the hernia changes
cues.why: The preceding explanation rehearses the change-of-policy boundary before this follow-up.

fairness: Elective repair assessment is defensible and the interval chronology is coherent. The current update is understandable independently of the earlier question.

The sequence contrasts the same observation-versus-referral rule twice. Repeat ultrasound has no new diagnostic uncertainty to resolve; continued surveillance ignores the clearly stated functional goal. These unsupported delays do not provide resident-level competition.
The new data matter to the answer, but a consequential second inference is not required in this option set.
suggestions: Retain the functional update but test a distinct remaining decision with credible competitors, or merge it into the initial symptom-attribution objective.
Remove 'Rehabilitation continues in every offered plan' unless it changes a real choice; it is editorial scaffolding in patient-facing text.

review.title: Interpret discordant superficial and deep responses to a nerve block
clarityIssues: 'Both symptoms return to their previous pattern' is imprecise after stating that the deep ache never changed; clarify that the burning returns while the deep ache persists.

cues.phrase: The superficial component has an injection-responsive contribution
cues.why: This is a near-tautological restatement of 'clothing no longer provokes burning' after injection.

cues.phrase: Both pain components are localized to the injected nerves
cues.why: The broad claim is contradicted directly by the unchanged deep ache.

cues.phrase: Neither pain component is informed by the injection
cues.why: The opposite extreme is contradicted directly by the improved burning, leaving the only cautious middle statement.

fairness: The keyed limited interpretation and explanation's specificity caveat are reasonable. The observation does not prove a unique nerve or justify a particular operation.
This tests reading a response pattern rather than two consequential clinical steps; 'both/neither/some' allows elimination without medical knowledge.
suggestions: Replace the extreme interpretations with comparably qualified, clinically plausible inferences about what the block can establish, and make that distinction affect a concrete next decision.
Keep the distinction between a responsive component and proof of a specific causal nerve.

review.title: Further imaging after an adequate negative dynamic groin study
clarityIssues: The explanation introduces 'the held mixed-pain MRI-versus-hip-versus-block question,' which is internal review context with no patient-facing meaning.

cues.phrase: Repeat the same dynamic groin ultrasound
cues.why: 'The same' advertises repetition of a fully acquired and reviewed study rather than a credible alternative acquisition.

cues.phrase: Examination reproduces no separate hip or adductor pain
cues.why: This explicitly removes the rationale for the hip-focused distractor.

fairness: Dynamic pelvic/groin MRI is a defensible next study for persistent unresolved symptoms after the described ultrasound. No confident clinical error identified.

The only new investigation aimed at the symptomatic region wins after the text disposes of both alternatives. Complete acquisition review is appropriate information, but this option set turns it into elimination rather than difficult interpretation.
suggestions: Use investigations with genuine competing indications and supply observations that distinguish their value; do not use an unchanged completed study as filler.
Remove internal held-item commentary from the explanation. Preserve acquisition adequacy and do not manufacture an indication to repeat imaging.

review.title: Threatened partial-circumference femoral bowel entrapment
fairness: Emergency exploration is the best offered intervention given fixed tenderness and substantially diminished bowel-wall enhancement. Stool passage does not make manual reduction or elective discharge appropriate.
The learner must reconcile preserved bowel transit with partial-wall entrapment, then recognize suspected ischemia and reject taxis. The misleadingly reassuring transit finding is consequential.
The hospital-review frame places initial support and surgical assessment at the correct care stage. The explanation appropriately distinguishes threatened viability from proven irreversible necrosis.
suggestions: Preserve both the partial-circumference anatomy and perfusion finding; do not remove urgency information to raise difficulty.

review.title: Symptomatic medial inguinal defect versus static cord fat
clarityIssues: 'Plan inguinal posterior-wall reinforcement' is less concrete than naming a repair operation; it can be confused with the posterior operative approach, which is a different distinction.

cues.phrase: displaces the canal wall
cues.why: This maps directly to the only wall-reinforcement option.

cues.phrase: Fat alongside the cord remains unchanged
cues.why: The static-versus-moving contrast makes isolated cord-fat excision an overtly mismatched target.

fairness: Repair assessment for a function-limiting reducing inguinal hernia is reasonable. No confident clinical error identified.

The direct-versus-indirect inference does not change the offered action: symptomatic inguinal defects can require repair regardless of that classification. Observation and isolated fat excision do not provide close management competitors here.
The explanation's statement that no unique mesh technique is established is appropriate, but does not cure the vague operative label.
suggestions: Use a specific clinically supported repair or planning decision in which the anatomical interpretation changes management, with same-stage alternatives.
Avoid implying that posterior-wall reinforcement specifies a posterior surgical approach.

review.title: Assess an unexamined new postoperative groin contour

cues.phrase: It contains no acquisition of the patient-marked repair site
cues.why: This names the missing action answered verbatim by targeted ultrasound.

cues.phrase: Groin ultrasound at the marked site during standing strain
cues.why: The key is substantially longer and carries the exact target/provocation correction; the other options are less specifically tailored.

fairness: Targeted dynamic ultrasound is a defensible initial evaluation of this new intermittent contour. The older adductor acquisition is not a negative study of the repair site.

An MRI is not intrinsically an incorrect investigation of postoperative groin symptoms; its lower priority here depends on the initial targeted-ultrasound sequence, not an assertion that it cannot evaluate recurrence.
The acquisition omission and highly specific key permit a language-level solution, despite the clinically useful intended distinction.
suggestions: Describe the acquisition record neutrally and balance target/protocol detail across all imaging choices. Require interpretation of what the earlier study actually establishes rather than naming a missing keyed action.
Keep the new pressure/contour separate from the older injection-responsive burning; do not replace that distinction with a diagnosis label.

review.title: Select the repair plane after an anterior mesh repair

cues.phrase: He has not had pelvic surgery or a preperitoneal repair
cues.why: The latter clause supplies the plane conclusion that the operative report should require the resident to infer.

cues.phrase: Open anterior Lichtenstein mesh repair
cues.why: Both distractors are explicitly labelled 'Open anterior'; the key is the only differently labelled approach, enhancing the unused-plane shortcut.

fairness: TEP is the best offered repair after the described anterior operation, with relevant expertise and no stated pelvic constraint. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.

The raw operative report could support two steps, but the explicit denial of a prior preperitoneal repair removes much of the first inference. The current item is straightforward opposite-plane recall.
suggestions: Remove the explicit prior-plane conclusion while retaining relevant surgical history. Let the operative anatomy establish the prior plane.
Use equally natural operation names and a credible surgical-history complication or competing interpretation if needed; do not invent contraindications simply to manufacture difficulty.

review.title: Recognize a prior open posterior repair before reoperation
fairness: The report describes posterior/preperitoneal mesh despite a groin incision. An offered anterior Lichtenstein repair follows the opposite-plane principle; both TAPP and TEP re-enter the used posterior compartment.
The two steps are interpretation of the actual mesh plane rather than the incision label, then selection of the opposite repair approach.

The follow-up coherently supplies the targeted study result and operative record. Its current update states the confirmed symptomatic recurrence and necessary history, so it stands alone. The earlier explanation teaches investigation adequacy, not this repair-plane answer.
suggestions: Preserve the open-incision versus actual-mesh-plane distinction and the explicit interval result.

review.title: Recurrent hernia after both operative compartments have been used
clarityIssues: The task asks for the next repair, but the key selects a referral/planning stage while the alternatives schedule specific operations.

cues.phrase: Refer for repair planning by a complex-hernia surgeon
cues.why: It is the only cautious specialist-planning answer between two immediate routine procedures.

cues.phrase: Schedule routine TEP repair in the ambulatory service
cues.why: 'Routine' and 'ambulatory service' advertise mismatch with repeated operations and dense scar; the Lichtenstein distractor uses the same framing.

fairness: Specialist planning is reasonable after failure in both compartments. The record does not establish one universally required repeat operation.
That appropriate uncertainty makes the referral key conspicuous. A reader can choose specialist assessment for the complex history without interpreting either operative plane.
suggestions: Compare concrete plans at the same care stage, removing 'routine' as a distractor warning label.
Make a supported observation change which specialist assessment or repair-planning step is needed. Do not force a unique operation where the evidence permits individualized expert management.

review.title: Elective repair approach in a woman with incompletely assessed groin anatomy

cues.phrase: its recorded field ends at that ligament
cues.why: The scan's missing coverage is stated explicitly, but it does not actually change the offered recommendation in this patient.

cues.phrase: She has no previous pelvic operation and can undergo general anesthesia
cues.why: This removes constraints to the single laparo-endoscopic option rather than introducing a competing interpretation.

fairness: TAPP is a defensible preferred offered approach for a nonpregnant woman in an experienced service; the explanation correctly avoids claiming superiority over TEP.
Deleting the entire ambiguous scan/neck description leaves essentially the same population-based recommendation. The exhibit-like anatomical information is therefore not a consequential first step.
The explanation relies on nonpregnancy; if that qualification is required for the teaching point, it should be explicit rather than inferred solely from age.
suggestions: Make a specific finding alter the planning decision, or revise the objective to the actual single population rule and seek an explicit basic-role exception.
Retain any genuine anesthesia/history constraints needed for fairness, but remove decorative anatomy. Clarify pregnancy status if clinically relevant to the option ranking.

review.title: Select an initial intervention for acute irreducibility without ischemic features
clarityIssues: 'Since a lifting episode' gives no elapsed chronology for the irreducible lump. The symptom course cannot be interpreted fully without knowing when the episode occurred.

cues.phrase: Monitored analgesia and surgical rescue are part of that service's care
cues.why: This previews the 'gentle monitored manual reduction' key. Monitored hospital care is legitimate safety context, but the phrase closely rehearses the offered intervention.

fairness: A monitored gentle reduction attempt is defensible when strangulation is not suspected; the stated absence of worsening pain, guarding, skin change or systemic deterioration supports that distinction.
The missing onset interval limits confidence in ranking taxis against immediate exploration. I am not asserting an absolute time cutoff or that elapsed duration by itself forbids reduction.

decisionNodes.explanation: Gross spillage separates this case from controlled clean-contaminated bowel resection. WSES supports primary tissue repair when such a defect is small and directly closable. Its less-than-3-cm boundary directly supports this constructed 2-cm observation; the recommendation is older and low certainty, not a rule for all contaminated abdominal-wall defects.
sourceLabels: WSES emergency complicated abdominal wall hernia guideline (2017)

terminalDispositions.consequenceNarrative: The teaching record selected Permanent macroporous synthetic mesh repair.
terminalDispositions.clinicalRationale: The permissive controlled-resection evidence cannot be carried over to gross contamination in a small directly closable defect.
sourceLabels: WSES emergency complicated abdominal wall hernia guideline (2017)

terminalDispositions.consequenceNarrative: The teaching record selected Biologic mesh reinforcement of the defect.
terminalDispositions.clinicalRationale: The cited older guideline reserves consideration of biologic material for contaminated defects where primary suture is not feasible; direct closure is feasible here.
sourceLabels: WSES emergency complicated abdominal wall hernia guideline (2017)

cases.presentation: Rafael Diaz, a 45-year-old man, attends the surgery clinic for groin evaluation.

approvedInstantiationProfiles.presentation: Rafael Diaz, a 45-year-old man, attends the surgery clinic for groin evaluation.

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: Rafael describes an ongoing ache within the right testicle after open inguinal repair. Pinprick and light touch over the groin and scrotal skin are symmetric and do not reproduce it. Gentle palpation of the testicle reproduces his usual ache. The groin scar is healed, and dynamic groin examination shows no impulse. There has been no sudden severe onset or systemic illness.
decisionNodes.stem: Which evaluation should next address Rafael's postrepair pain?

answerChoices.label: Urological assessment of the scrotal contents

decisionNodes.explanation: Rafael's symptom is reproduced in the testicular contents rather than the scrotal skin. HerniaSurge distinguishes those sources and supports formal urological evaluation for orchialgia. A prior hernia operation does not establish that a cutaneous nerve block or mesh removal addresses this pain.

terminalDispositions.consequenceNarrative: The teaching record selected Genital-branch block with cutaneous mapping.
terminalDispositions.clinicalRationale: A skin nerve target is not established by pain reproduced within the testicle while the skin examination is unremarkable.

terminalDispositions.consequenceNarrative: The teaching record selected Hernia-surgery assessment for mesh removal.
terminalDispositions.clinicalRationale: The current record does not establish mesh as the source. Evaluate the symptomatic contents before selecting a mesh-directed intervention.

cases.presentation: Evan Carter, a 78-year-old man, attends the surgery clinic for groin evaluation.

approvedInstantiationProfiles.presentation: Evan Carter, a 78-year-old man, attends the surgery clinic for groin evaluation.

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: Evan has a unilateral reducing inguinal hernia that interrupts dressing and walking. He has severe chronic pulmonary disease without a current exacerbation and previously needed catheterization after spinal anesthesia. The team plans an open Lichtenstein repair. He can cooperate during the procedure, and the team routinely uses both local and general techniques for this operation.
decisionNodes.stem: Which anesthetic approach should be favored for Evan's planned open inguinal repair?
decisionNodes.explanation: For an experienced team's open repair of a reducing inguinal hernia, local anesthesia is supported and can benefit frail patients. Evan's pulmonary disease and prior retention make an automatic switch to general or spinal anesthesia less attractive. No drug, dose or universal anesthetic contraindication is authored.

terminalDispositions.consequenceNarrative: The teaching record selected Spinal anesthesia.
terminalDispositions.clinicalRationale: Regional anesthesia is not the favored alternative in this older frail patient with prior retention. Local open repair is an established option with appropriate expertise.

terminalDispositions.consequenceNarrative: The teaching record selected General anesthesia.
terminalDispositions.clinicalRationale: General anesthesia is possible, but the severe pulmonary comorbidity, cooperative patient and experienced local-repair team support favoring local anesthesia here.

cases.presentation: Aisha Wilson, a 31-year-old woman, attends the surgery clinic for groin evaluation. She is 26 weeks pregnant.

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: Aisha is pregnant and has painless right groin fullness that increases while standing and empties supine. Color Doppler shows compressible serpiginous channels along the round ligament with venous flow augmented during strain. Repeated dynamic views show no protruding bowel or fat sac. She has no acute pain, erythema or vomiting.
decisionNodes.stem: Which groin plan should be recommended for Aisha at this clinic review?

answerChoices.label: Arrange elective preperitoneal hernia repair during pregnancy
Arrange operative excision of the inguinal swelling
Observe the groin swelling with return precautions

decisionNodes.explanation: The observed venous channels support round-ligament varicosities, not a demonstrated bowel/fat hernia sac. Uncomplicated pregnancy-associated swelling can be observed with reassessment for new symptoms. The supporting literature is small-cohort/case-series evidence and does not justify ignoring a painful or compromised groin finding.

definitions.name: Elena Ortiz
definitions.presentation: Elena Ortiz, a 48-year-old woman, attends the surgery clinic for groin evaluation.

nodes.identityReason: Same stable femoral repair-versus-observation meaning; new anatomical evidence and credible competing attribution.
nodes.objective: Identify which of two groin findings accounts for the marked swelling before choosing repair or surveillance.
nodes.currentUpdate: Elena marks the lump she notices while standing. It empties when she lies down and is nontender. She is eating normally without vomiting.

exhibit.caption: Original constructed teaching record; fictional observations

items.label: At Elena's marker
items.value: A sac containing bowel passes below the inguinal ligament, immediately medial to the common femoral vein.

items.label: Separate cranial finding
items.value: Fat protrudes above the ligament, medial to the inferior epigastric vessels; pressing here does not reproduce the marked lump.

nodes.stem: Which plan should be recommended for Elena's marked groin swelling?

choices.label: Schedule groin surveillance
choices.rationale: Painless reduction does not place a femoral hernia in the selected-male inguinal observation population.
choices.temptation: Overgeneralize observation from painless inguinal hernias.
choices.counterfactual: A minimally symptomatic reducible inguinal hernia in a man would permit informed observation.

choices.label: Arrange elective groin repair
choices.rationale: The marked sac follows the femoral compartment. Its stable reducing course supports elective repair assessment rather than emergency exploration.
choices.temptation: Integrate the marked target, anatomical neck and present acuity.
choices.counterfactual: New fixed tenderness or suspected ischemia would change the urgency.

choices.label: Arrange emergency groin exploration
choices.rationale: Femoral anatomy supports repair but does not by itself establish an acute ischemic emergency in this reducing, nontender presentation.
choices.temptation: Translate higher complication concern into emergency treatment for every femoral defect.
choices.counterfactual: An acutely irreducible tender sac with compromised bowel enhancement would support emergency exploration.

nodes.explanation: The marked swelling follows the femoral route; the separate cranial direct defect does not explain that target. A femoral hernia warrants timely elective repair assessment despite little discomfort. Current reduction and absence of acute illness determine the elective rather than emergency pathway.

gate.interpret: Localize the neck of the marked sac rather than anchoring on a second visible defect.
gate.apply: Apply the femoral repair boundary and current acuity to select an elective plan.
gate.cueAttack: Removed the named femoral diagnosis from the complaint and vignette. All choices are groin-care plans; the key is not a longer combined plan. Necessary reducing/nontender observations distinguish urgency.
gate.stageCategory: Current groin management, three concrete policies.
gate.difficulty: Predicted moderate: the painless reducing course and incidental cranial defect tempt surveillance or wrong-target attribution.
gate.decidingObservation: The sac at the marker is below the ligament and medial to the vein, and currently reduces.
gate.counterfactual: Move the marked sac above the ligament into the inguinal compartment in a minimally symptomatic man: surveillance becomes reasonable. Add irreducibility and ischemia concern: emergency exploration.
gate.deletionTest: The separate defect earns its place by competing for attribution; removing compartment or reduction observations makes the repair/urgency choice underdetermined.
gate.sequenceCheck: Standalone; neither a prior type label nor a companion explanation supplies the classification.

definitions.name: Daniel Brooks
definitions.presentation: Daniel Brooks, a 46-year-old man, attends the surgery clinic for groin evaluation.

nodes.identityReason: Preserves the selected-male observation boundary; a task-specific activity record replaces the supplied minimally symptomatic interpretation.
nodes.objective: Use current function and symptom concordance to decide whether immediate elective inguinal repair is necessary.
nodes.currentUpdate: Daniel's scan shows a right inguinal sac that enters during strain and reduces at rest. He completes his usual warehouse lifts while the contour is visible, without groin pressure. The pain that stops running is medial to the pubis and is reproduced by resisted adduction. He prefers to defer an operation if reasonable.
nodes.stem: Which inguinal-hernia plan should be offered to Daniel at this review?

choices.label: Repeat dynamic groin ultrasound before planning
choices.rationale: The diagnosis and reduction are already established; there is no unresolved acquisition or anatomy question here.
choices.temptation: Seek another image because there is pain somewhere in the groin.
choices.counterfactual: A reported lump outside the acquired field would support a targeted repeat study.

choices.label: Arrange elective inguinal repair now
choices.rationale: Repair can be discussed, but attributing the current running limitation to this painless protrusion is unsupported. The requested plan incorporates Daniel's preference to defer.
choices.temptation: Treat any positive image in a patient with pain as a symptomatic surgical target.
choices.counterfactual: Lifting interrupted by pressure at the protrusion that resolves on reduction would favor repair planning.

choices.label: Continue hernia observation with return precautions
choices.rationale: A man completing usual activity without protrusion-related limitation can choose informed observation. The separate attachment pain does not automatically negate that option.
choices.temptation: Distinguish the activity-limiting symptom from a coexisting reducible hernia.
choices.counterfactual: A new painful nonreducing lump would require urgent assessment rather than continued observation.

nodes.explanation: Daniel's limiting pain is dissociated from the protrusion during the activity actually attempted. Informed observation is a reasonable hernia policy under his stated preference, with return precautions and reassessment if the hernia changes. This does not dismiss the separate painful condition or guarantee that symptoms will remain mild.

gate.interpret: Compare the pain that stops running with painless completion of the original lifting task.
gate.apply: Apply the selected-male inguinal observation boundary and preference after that attribution.
gate.cueAttack: All choices are hernia policies; no option says individualized. The task names the inguinal plan so it does not ask the learner to rank an unsupported hip regimen. A patient preference is necessary because repair remains a reasonable elective choice.
gate.stageCategory: Current hernia policy after diagnostic confirmation.
gate.difficulty: Predicted moderate: a positive scan plus pain tempts immediate repair, while repeating imaging feels cautious.
gate.decidingObservation: Usual lifting is completed with the contour present, while a separate maneuver reproduces the limiting medial pain.
gate.counterfactual: Replace painless lifting with load interruption during protrusion and relief on reduction: elective repair becomes the best offered policy.
gate.deletionTest: Without actual usual-load performance, symptom location or preference, observation versus elective repair becomes less determinate.
gate.sequenceCheck: First node of a later-change pair. Feedback gives no later examination, interval response or specific future referral trigger.

nodes.identityReason: Preserves interval function and symptom attribution, without transferring it to the older broader symptomatic-repair identities.
nodes.objective: Reassess a prior observation plan when the functional limitation changes despite improvement of a competing pain source.
nodes.currentUpdate: At a later clinic visit, Daniel completes resisted adduction and his running program without the earlier medial pain. During a trial of his usual warehouse lift, focal inguinal pressure makes him put the load down as the lump appears. The pressure resolves when the lump reduces. He wants to resume this task. Rehabilitation continues in every offered plan.
nodes.stem: Which hernia-care policy should now be offered for Daniel's warehouse lifting limitation?

choices.label: Arrange elective inguinal repair assessment
choices.rationale: The remaining original-task restriction now tracks protrusion and reduction despite recovery of the earlier attachment symptom.
choices.temptation: Update attribution rather than preserving the old observation plan by inertia.
choices.counterfactual: If usual lifts were painless and completed with the contour present, observation would remain reasonable.

choices.label: Continue scheduled inguinal hernia surveillance
choices.rationale: Completed exercise does not establish recovery of the original load-bearing task, which is now interrupted by a concordant hernia episode.
choices.temptation: Use improving running as evidence that all groin function has recovered.
choices.counterfactual: Painless completion of usual work with the reducing contour could support observation.

choices.label: Repeat dynamic groin ultrasound before referral
choices.rationale: A demonstrated hernia and currently reproduced reduction-responsive restriction support consultation without requiring another identical confirmation.
choices.temptation: Require anatomical growth before considering a symptomatic hernia for repair.
choices.counterfactual: A new lump in a different compartment or an unestablished diagnosis would justify targeted imaging.

nodes.explanation: The new functional record changes the earlier symptom attribution. The original load now produces a focal, reduction-responsive episode while the earlier attachment pain has improved. Elective hernia assessment is supported without promising that surgery treats every future groin symptom.

gate.interpret: Separate actual recovery of running from failure of the usual warehouse lift.
gate.apply: Change the hernia policy for concordant current limitation, rather than demanding scan progression.
gate.cueAttack: Deleted generic treatment-priority labels and kept rehabilitation common. Three concrete hernia policies have similar scope. The observation is raw performance, not an author declaration of symptomatic hernia.
gate.stageCategory: Hernia management after interval functional reassessment.
gate.difficulty: Predicted moderate: prior successful observation and improved exercise compete with the new original-load failure.
gate.decidingObservation: Pressure arises with the protrusion during the attempted usual lift and resolves on reduction.
gate.counterfactual: Change the attempted lift to painless completion despite the contour: observation becomes reasonable.
gate.deletionTest: Removing the interval update restores the prior observation answer; this later node earns an independent changed inference.
gate.sequenceCheck: Earlier feedback explains the earlier observation but cannot supply the new load test, new preference or recovery of attachment pain. No future repair technique is taught here.

definitions.name: Mara Lewis
definitions.presentation: Mara Lewis, a 43-year-old woman, attends the surgery clinic for groin evaluation. She is reviewing pain after an open inguinal repair.

nodes.identityReason: New meaning: interpret component-specific block evidence, rather than select a block because a target exists. Preserve old FSRS history.
nodes.objective: Interpret selective relief of one pain component without converting it into proof that all postoperative pain has one cause.
nodes.currentUpdate: Before injection, Mara recorded superficial burning with clothing contact and a separate deep ache on stairs. After an ultrasound-guided ilioinguinal/iliohypogastric block, pinprick is reduced over the intended skin region and clothing no longer provokes burning. Stair climbing still produces the same deep ache. Both symptoms return to their previous pattern as the block wears off.
nodes.stem: Which interpretation of Mara's diagnostic block is best supported?

choices.label: Both pain components are localized to the injected nerves
choices.rationale: The stair-related ache persisted despite the observed skin sensory change. Response of one component does not localize every symptom.
choices.temptation: Count any relief as confirmation of a single nerve explanation.
choices.counterfactual: A reproducible response of both components would support a broader contribution, while still not guaranteeing surgery success.

choices.label: The superficial component has an injection-responsive contribution
choices.rationale: The temporally matched cutaneous sensory and clothing response supports that component, while the unchanged deep ache remains unresolved. It does not uniquely prove a particular injured nerve.
choices.temptation: Use component-specific response instead of an all-or-none label.
choices.counterfactual: If neither intended sensory change nor superficial relief occurred, a localized response could not be inferred.

choices.label: Neither pain component is informed by the injection
choices.rationale: Dismissing the observed superficial response loses valid local information because another symptom persists.
choices.temptation: Treat an incomplete overall response as a wholly useless test.
choices.counterfactual: No target sensory effect or symptom change would make this block nondiagnostic for localization.

nodes.explanation: The block informs the superficial component and leaves the stair-related deep ache unresolved. Block responses have limited specificity and can reflect overlapping targets or nonspecific effects. This result neither establishes a single cause for both symptoms nor selects a particular operation.

gate.interpret: Compare the observed sensory effect and clothing response with the unchanged stair symptom.
gate.apply: Limit localization to the responsive component without dismissing useful local evidence.
gate.cueAttack: Replaced supportive information versus absurd infection/recurrence claims with three equally scoped interpretations. The key avoids the uniquely cautious umbrella plan. No surgical selection is embedded in the stem.
gate.stageCategory: Interpretation of an acquired diagnostic response; three component-scope conclusions.
gate.difficulty: Predicted moderate: both overgeneralizing a partial response and discarding it are credible errors.
gate.decidingObservation: Superficial symptom relief accompanies the intended skin sensory effect, while the deep symptom is unchanged.
gate.counterfactual: Remove target sensory change and symptom relief: a localized injection-responsive contribution is no longer established.
gate.deletionTest: Both before/after component observations are necessary; deleting the deep symptom removes the main localization boundary.
gate.sequenceCheck: First node of the chronic-pain pair. Feedback does not supply a minimum treatment interval or the later treatment response.

nodes.identityReason: New readiness for invasive chronic-pain treatment, distinct from block interpretation or nerve localization.
nodes.objective: Distinguish elapsed time since repair from an adequate trial of structured chronic-pain treatment.
nodes.currentUpdate: At later review, Mara is eight months after open repair. Her wound is healed, repeated targeted examination has not demonstrated recurrence, and pain still limits work. She entered a specialist hernia/pain program two weeks ago, with medication adjustment and injection therapy. She asks for an operation because so much time has passed since repair. No intolerable treatment adverse effect or progressive focal deficit is recorded.
nodes.stem: Which treatment plan should be recommended for Mara at this later review?

choices.label: Proceed to open triple neurectomy
choices.rationale: Passing a postoperative interval is not the same as completing the recommended period of less invasive pain treatment. The available record does not select triple neurectomy now.
choices.temptation: Use the date of the original repair as the sole escalation criterion.
choices.counterfactual: Persistent carefully characterized pain after an adequate specialist treatment course may warrant discussion of tailored surgery, without automatically selecting triple neurectomy.

choices.label: Continue the specialist nonoperative pain program
choices.rationale: The structured trial has just begun. HerniaSurge suggests continuing pharmacologic/interventional measures for at least three months and being at least six months from repair before invasive treatment planning.
choices.temptation: Interpret treatment exposure as well as time since repair.
choices.counterfactual: Persistent disabling pain after a completed adequate treatment course would justify a new multidisciplinary discussion of invasive options.

choices.label: Proceed to anterior mesh explantation
choices.rationale: The record supplies neither a specific mesh complication requiring removal nor an adequate completed conservative course. Mesh removal is not selected by postoperative duration alone.
choices.temptation: Attribute all chronic postrepair pain to implanted material.
choices.counterfactual: A documented mesh-related complication after adequate evaluation may support tailored expert surgery, with its risks considered.

nodes.explanation: Mara has passed the postoperative interval but has only begun structured pain treatment. Continue the specialist pharmacologic/interventional program and reassess. The guideline's minimum intervals do not establish that surgery becomes mandatory after they pass, and any future operation requires individualized evidence and counseling about failure or worsened pain.

gate.interpret: Distinguish eight months since repair from two weeks in the actual structured treatment program.
gate.apply: Apply readiness for invasive escalation, retaining specialist care rather than selecting a fixed operation.
gate.cueAttack: The previous partial block response is not reinterpreted as a surgical indication. Three concrete treatment policies at the same decision phase; exact clinical intervals are sourced, not diagnostic wait durations.
gate.stageCategory: Escalation of chronic postoperative pain treatment after recurrence assessment.
gate.difficulty: Predicted moderate: elapsed postoperative time and prior partial block response tempt premature surgery.
gate.decidingObservation: The pain program has lasted two weeks despite eight months since repair.
gate.counterfactual: Supply an adequate completed specialist treatment course with persistent disabling symptoms: reconsider invasive planning; the exact operation still requires new evidence.
gate.deletionTest: Deleting either interval hides the tested distinction. The lack of progressive deficit/urgent complication preserves a fair conservative-versus-invasive comparison.
gate.sequenceCheck: Prior feedback limits block localization and does not supply the later treatment interval. The new treatment-exposure record is essential to this node.

definitions.name: Priya Shah
definitions.presentation: Priya Shah, a 52-year-old woman, attends the surgery clinic for groin evaluation.

nodes.identityReason: Same adequacy-dependent escalation meaning, narrowed to avoid ranking MRI over an unresolved symptomatic hip or block.
nodes.objective: Choose the next investigation after an adequately targeted negative dynamic study when episodic groin anatomy remains unresolved.
nodes.currentUpdate: Priya's patient-marked swelling was scanned by an experienced examiner supine and standing during cough and Valsalva; the contour and familiar pressure occurred during recording, without a demonstrable sac. The complete acquisition and cine loops have been reviewed. Examination reproduces no separate hip or adductor pain. The episodes continue to stop her lifting.
nodes.stem: Which investigation should next assess Priya's unresolved episodic groin swelling?

choices.label: Repeat the same dynamic groin ultrasound
choices.rationale: The symptomatic target, provocation and complete acquisition have already been adequately assessed. A different acquisition would be reasonable if those conditions were missing.
choices.temptation: Repeat a familiar first-line study without identifying a new target or acquisition defect.
choices.counterfactual: If the previous worksheet documented an adductor-only examination, targeted dynamic groin ultrasound would become the best option.

choices.label: Obtain pelvic MRI with groin strain acquisitions
choices.rationale: Persistent diagnostic uncertainty after an adequate examination and ultrasound supports dynamic cross-sectional assessment. No claim is made that it will resolve every pain source.
choices.temptation: Escalate because of genuine residual uncertainty after an adequate first investigation.
choices.counterfactual: An unexamined symptomatic site would favor a properly targeted ultrasound first.

choices.label: Obtain hip MRI with intra-articular contrast
choices.rationale: The represented unresolved event is an intermittent groin contour, not a clinically reproduced hip-joint problem requiring this acquisition.
choices.temptation: Treat every deep groin symptom as an intra-articular hip disorder.
choices.counterfactual: Usual pain reproduced by hip rotation with mechanical joint symptoms and no contour question would support a hip-directed pathway.

nodes.explanation: The actual target and provocation were acquired, so this is not a missing-view or wrong-site negative. Persistent anatomical uncertainty can justify dynamic MRI. The narrowed case provides no competing reproduced hip symptom and does not resolve the held mixed-pain MRI-versus-hip-versus-block question.

gate.interpret: Use acquisition records, symptom reproduction and complete loops to judge what the negative study evaluated.
gate.apply: Select cross-sectional dynamic assessment for the remaining anatomical question.
gate.cueAttack: Removed available-MRI permission and the supplied inadequate/adequate label. All choices are named imaging protocols with wait metadata. Preserved actual acquisition rather than treating missing exports as unperformed maneuvers.
gate.stageCategory: Next imaging after a reviewed negative symptomatic acquisition.
gate.difficulty: Predicted moderate: protocol adequacy makes repeating ultrasound versus advancing to MRI consequential. One-guideline source limitation remains.
gate.decidingObservation: The correct marked target and clinical event were recorded during a complete dynamic examination, yet no sac was shown.
gate.counterfactual: Change the recorded acquisition to a different tender attachment at rest: repeat targeted groin ultrasound becomes preferred.
gate.deletionTest: Deleting the acquisition record removes the reason not to repeat ultrasound. Hip observations earn their role because a hip protocol is offered, but no hip symptom is suppressed from an actual patient.
gate.sequenceCheck: Standalone, independent of the frozen proximal-neck workup. Does not alter any approved/PASS companion.

definitions.name: Andre Silva
definitions.presentation: Andre Silva, a 59-year-old man, is the named patient in an outside-hospital chart review requested at the surgery clinic.

nodes.identityReason: Same compartment-plus-wall-viability intervention meaning; change the original ultrasound observations to supported CT observations and use a hospital chart-review frame.
nodes.objective: Apply partial-wall anatomy and impaired enhancement to select operative evaluation despite continued stool passage.
nodes.currentUpdate: The referring hospital reports a newly fixed tender right groin lump. Andre still passes stool and has not vomited. Contrast CT shows part of the bowel circumference entering a small opening below the inguinal ligament, medial to the common femoral vein. The remaining lumen stays in the abdomen. The trapped wall enhances substantially less than adjacent bowel. Initial IV support and surgical consultation are underway.
nodes.stem: Which hernia-directed intervention should be recommended for Andre's current hospital episode?

choices.label: Attempt manual reduction with analgesia
choices.rationale: Continued passage does not exclude wall compromise when only part of the circumference is trapped. Tender fixation and reduced enhancement raise ischemia concern.
choices.temptation: Use absence of complete obstruction to declare reduction safe.
choices.counterfactual: An acutely irreducible sac with no ischemic concern may be considered for gentle reduction by the hospital team.

choices.label: Plan elective repair after discharge
choices.rationale: The current episode contains fixed tenderness and compromised enhancement, not an uncomplicated reducing femoral hernia.
choices.temptation: Apply the elective femoral pathway despite changed acuity.
choices.counterfactual: A nontender sac that empties at rest without ischemic findings would support elective planning.

choices.label: Proceed to emergency operative exploration
choices.rationale: The anatomy is femoral and the partial-wall pattern permits continued lumen passage despite threatened tissue. Suspected strangulation supports emergency surgery.
choices.temptation: Prioritize tissue viability over stool passage as reassurance.
choices.counterfactual: If the sac reduced and the wall had normal enhancement with resolving symptoms, this immediate exploration comparison would change.

nodes.explanation: Only part of the circumference is trapped, so stool passage is compatible with threatened wall. The femoral compartment, fixed tenderness and reduced enhancement support suspected strangulation and emergency operative evaluation rather than taxis. This does not claim that CT alone proves irreversible necrosis or choose a repair material.

gate.interpret: Recognize that preserved lumen passage and partial-wall entrapment can coexist.
gate.apply: Interpret reduced wall enhancement and tender fixation as a contraindication to attempted reduction in this offered comparison.
gate.cueAttack: Neutral intervention task, three specific hernia plans; shared IV support stays common. No named Richter/strangulation diagnosis is provided. The continuing stool detail creates the closest error, not decorative reassurance.
gate.stageCategory: Hernia intervention in an outside-hospital episode reviewed from clinic.
gate.difficulty: Predicted moderate to hard: false reassurance from intestinal passage competes with the wall-specific perfusion and acute examination.
gate.decidingObservation: The trapped wall enhances less than adjacent bowel despite the residual abdominal lumen.
gate.counterfactual: Replace compromised enhancement and acute fixed tenderness with an uncomplicated reducible sac: planned elective repair becomes appropriate.
gate.deletionTest: Removing partial-wall geometry makes stool passage less interpretable; removing enhancement and tender fixation removes the main reduction-versus-exploration boundary.
gate.sequenceCheck: First node of a hospital-record sequence. Feedback does not name later contamination, mesh material or wound class.

nodes.identityReason: New groin repair-material eligibility after bowel resection; distinct from the urgency construct.
nodes.objective: Distinguish controlled bowel resection from gross enteric contamination before excluding permanent mesh.
nodes.currentUpdate: At the next clinic chart review, Andre's operative record documents removal of the nonviable trapped bowel and a closed anastomosis. The resection was controlled without enteric spillage. The surgeon reports no perforation, pus or peritonitis, and stable circulation. The remaining decision in the record is how to reinforce the groin defect.
nodes.stem: Which repair policy is supported by Andre's recorded operative field?

choices.label: Defer groin reinforcement to a later operation
choices.rationale: Controlled resection without gross contamination does not require a routine staged groin repair.
choices.temptation: Treat any intestinal procedure as incompatible with definitive hernia repair.
choices.counterfactual: Severe instability or an uncontrolled contaminated field could require a staged strategy.

choices.label: Allow permanent macroporous synthetic mesh repair
choices.rationale: A controlled clean-contaminated resection is not an automatic exclusion of macroporous permanent synthetic mesh. This is eligibility, not a claim that every patient must receive it.
choices.temptation: Classify the actual contamination rather than using resection as a surrogate.
choices.counterfactual: Gross enteric spillage with a small closable defect would change the preferred policy toward tissue repair.

choices.label: Restrict groin reinforcement to primary tissue repair
choices.rationale: Tissue repair remains possible, but excluding permanent mesh solely because bowel was resected is unsupported in the represented controlled field.
choices.temptation: Overgeneralize a contaminated-field restriction to all bowel resections.
choices.counterfactual: Gross contamination with a small defect suitable for direct closure supports a primary tissue strategy.

nodes.explanation: The relevant boundary is the actual operative field, not bowel resection as a binary label. Current HerniaSurge guidance allows macroporous mesh after a controlled clean-contaminated resection; older WSES guidance supports the same eligibility. This weak-evidence comparison does not mandate one material or extend to gross spillage.

gate.interpret: Classify controlled resection without spillage as a different field from enteric contamination.
gate.apply: Decide whether permanent mesh must be excluded, without inventing universal operative superiority.
gate.cueAttack: Repaired an initial material-versus-material ambiguity by asking an eligibility policy. All labels are actual repair policies, without rationale text. The key does not say safe, best or no infection risk.
gate.stageCategory: Definitive groin reinforcement policy after completed source management.
gate.difficulty: Predicted moderate to hard: bowel resection often prompts blanket mesh avoidance, while the field changes that boundary.
gate.decidingObservation: Controlled resection with no spillage, perforation, pus or peritonitis.
gate.counterfactual: Add gross stool spillage and a small closable defect: primary tissue repair becomes the supported policy.
gate.deletionTest: Deleting the field observations leaves only bowel resection and makes mesh eligibility underdetermined.
gate.sequenceCheck: Earlier acute feedback discusses viability and urgency, not wound class or repair material. This later operative record earns a distinct inference.

definitions.name: Owen Reed
definitions.presentation: Owen Reed, a 63-year-old man, attends the surgery clinic for groin evaluation.
