choices.counterfactual: Recurrence after a prior posterior TEP/TAPP repair would favor an anterior approach.

choices.label: Totally extraperitoneal mesh repair
choices.rationale: The old record describes anterior mesh placement. The offered TEP accesses the posterior compartment for recurrence after anterior mesh repair.
choices.temptation: Translate mesh location into the previously used compartment and select the opposite plane.
choices.counterfactual: A prior posterior repair would change the preferred offered approach to anterior repair.

choices.label: Open anterior Shouldice tissue repair
choices.rationale: Avoiding new mesh does not avoid the old anterior dissection or establish a tissue-repair preference for this recurrence.
choices.temptation: Mistake the material choice for a change in surgical plane.
choices.counterfactual: A selected primary inguinal hernia with an informed non-mesh preference could be considered for expert Shouldice repair.

nodes.explanation: Mesh on the inguinal floor beneath the cord and external oblique identifies the prior anterior repair. An offered posterior repair is recommended for this recurrence. This ranks TEP against two anterior options, not against TAPP or every other posterior operation.

gate.interpret: Identify the operated compartment from tissue relationships rather than the incision name.
gate.apply: Choose the offered posterior repair for a recurrence after anterior mesh repair.
gate.cueAttack: Removed the intraoperative pause and implied immediate conversion. All options are named repairs. The surgeon's competence applies to every offered approach and is needed for a fair technique comparison.
gate.stageCategory: Elective repair selection in clinic, before an operation has begun.
gate.difficulty: Predicted moderate: tissue material versus plane and old mesh location create credible competing errors.
gate.decidingObservation: Old mesh lies on the floor with cord and external oblique superficial to it.
gate.counterfactual: Move old mesh to the space behind transversalis fascia after TEP/TAPP: Lichtenstein becomes the offered preferred approach.
gate.deletionTest: Without prior mesh relationships the recurrence plane cannot be inferred; prior pelvic history constrains use of TEP.
gate.sequenceCheck: Standalone; no earlier repair-referral explanation names the plane. Does not alter the passed B2A05 question or presentation.

nodes.identityReason: New complementary recurrence-plane construct; the existing anterior-to-posterior identity is not repurposed.
nodes.objective: Infer a prior posterior repair from an open operative record and choose an anterior approach for recurrence.
nodes.currentUpdate: At a later clinic review, Victor's targeted study demonstrates a reducing recurrent inguinal sac at the site of the lifting episode. The retrieved operation report describes an incision in the groin, division through the transversalis fascia, and a flat mesh unfolded between that fascia and the peritoneum to cover the myopectineal orifice. There was no earlier mesh on the inguinal floor. The offered operations are within the consulting team's experience.
nodes.stem: Which repair should be offered for Victor's confirmed symptomatic recurrence?

choices.label: Transabdominal preperitoneal mesh repair
choices.rationale: TAPP reenters the previously dissected posterior compartment despite the old operation having used an open skin incision.
choices.temptation: Treat open skin access as proof that the previous mesh was anterior.
choices.counterfactual: A recurrence after a prior anterior Lichtenstein repair would favor a posterior approach.

choices.label: Open anterior Lichtenstein mesh repair
choices.rationale: The tissue relationships identify a prior posterior preperitoneal mesh. An anterior repair uses the other plane.
choices.temptation: Distinguish surgical access from implanted mesh compartment.
choices.counterfactual: If old mesh lay on the floor beneath the cord and external oblique, an offered posterior repair would be preferred.

choices.label: Totally extraperitoneal mesh repair
choices.rationale: TEP also revisits the operated posterior space; changing transabdominal to extraperitoneal access does not change the mesh compartment.
choices.temptation: Treat TEP and TAPP as opposite tissue planes.
choices.counterfactual: An anterior-only prior repair would make TEP a reasonable posterior option.

nodes.explanation: An open incision does not identify the mesh plane. The report places mesh behind transversalis fascia and before peritoneum, so the posterior compartment has already been used. The offered anterior Lichtenstein repair follows the opposite-plane recurrence principle.

gate.interpret: Read tissue relationships to identify posterior mesh despite an open incision.
gate.apply: Choose anterior recurrence repair, distinguishing plane from TEP/TAPP access.
gate.cueAttack: Three named mesh repairs, comparable scope and wording. No supplied anterior/posterior label. Both posterior distractors are credible because the incision and access names can mislead.
gate.stageCategory: Elective recurrence operation selection after confirmation.
gate.difficulty: Predicted moderate to hard: misclassifying an open preperitoneal repair is a practical resident error.
gate.decidingObservation: The old mesh lies between transversalis fascia and peritoneum rather than on the inguinal floor.
gate.counterfactual: Place the old mesh under external oblique and superficial to fascia: either offered posterior method becomes reasonable, so the present Lichtenstein key no longer wins.
gate.deletionTest: Deleting the old operative anatomy makes the procedure comparison unfair. The new positive scan earns the transition from investigation to repair planning.
gate.sequenceCheck: Previous feedback concerns scan target and pain attribution, with no recurrence-plane rule. This new record and result add a distinct surgical decision.

nodes.identityReason: New complex recurrent-repair referral boundary, distinct from either simple opposite-plane rule.
nodes.objective: Recognize that two prior operations have used both planes before choosing where to plan another repair.
nodes.currentUpdate: Sofia's recurrent groin protrusion again interrupts work but reduces when she lies down. One old report records mesh on the inguinal floor under the external oblique. A later report records removal of part of that mesh and placement of a second prosthesis behind the transversalis fascia. Both reports describe dense scar around the round-ligament region. There is no fixed tenderness, vomiting or abdominal distension.
nodes.stem: Which plan should be offered for Sofia's next recurrent groin repair?

choices.label: Schedule routine TEP repair in the ambulatory service
choices.rationale: The posterior compartment has already been entered and implanted; it cannot be presumed to be an unused rescue plane.
choices.temptation: Apply anterior-to-posterior repair as if only the first report mattered.
choices.counterfactual: An anterior-only prior repair with an untouched posterior space could support an experienced team's TEP repair.

choices.label: Refer for repair planning by a complex-hernia surgeon
choices.rationale: Both compartments have been operated on. Expert recurrent-hernia assessment is recommended rather than selecting a universally preferred repeat route.
choices.temptation: Integrate both archived operations before applying a repair rule.
choices.counterfactual: One clearly anterior prior mesh repair with an unused posterior plane would make routine posterior planning reasonable.

choices.label: Schedule routine Lichtenstein repair in the ambulatory service
choices.rationale: The anterior compartment is also scarred and implanted. The simple posterior-to-anterior rule does not resolve a recurrence after both approaches.
choices.temptation: Treat only the most recent posterior repair as relevant.
choices.counterfactual: A posterior-only failed repair could support experienced anterior repair.

nodes.explanation: The two reports document use of both compartments. This is beyond a simple opposite-plane recurrence. A complex-hernia surgeon should plan the next repair; the evidence does not support one mandatory repeat operation for every such patient.

gate.interpret: Combine both reports instead of classifying only the last operation.
gate.apply: Recognize that neither standard route represents a reliably unused plane and escalate operative planning to specialist expertise.
gate.cueAttack: The referral key competes with concrete repeat repairs, so its caution is necessary only because both planes are documented. No claim of impossible local surgery or universal technique superiority is made.
gate.stageCategory: Planning responsibility for a multiply recurrent hernia, all options are concrete repair pathways.
gate.difficulty: Predicted moderate: recency anchoring and automatic opposite-plane rules compete. Independent review should check that referral remains a consequential decision rather than a generic cautious key.
gate.decidingObservation: Mesh is recorded both on the inguinal floor and behind transversalis fascia in separate operations.
gate.counterfactual: Delete the posterior operation: a posterior repair becomes reasonable. Delete the anterior operation: anterior repair becomes reasonable.
gate.deletionTest: Both reports are necessary to defeat each simple repair rule; stable reduction keeps the task elective.
gate.sequenceCheck: Standalone; not immediately paired with a simple recurrence-plane item that rehearses both rules.

nodes.identityReason: New female repair-coverage objective, beyond named hernia classification or repair urgency.
nodes.objective: Select an approach that examines and covers possible femoral disease in a nonpregnant woman with incompletely characterized groin anatomy.
nodes.currentUpdate: Lydia's painful but reducible right groin lump interrupts walking. The outside scan records a sac beside the round ligament above the inguinal ligament; its recorded field ends at that ligament. On standing examination the visible fullness extends across the crease, and the neck is difficult to palpate. She has no previous pelvic operation and can undergo general anesthesia. The consulting service regularly performs the offered repairs.
nodes.stem: Which elective repair should be discussed for Lydia's groin hernia?

choices.label: Open anterior Lichtenstein mesh repair
choices.rationale: It can repair inguinal disease, but the represented uncertainty in a woman includes a femoral compartment that an anterior inguinal repair may overlook.
choices.temptation: Accept the outside inguinal label as complete anatomical coverage.
choices.counterfactual: A patient requiring local anesthesia with adequately characterized inguinal anatomy could favor an experienced anterior repair.

choices.label: Transabdominal preperitoneal mesh repair
choices.rationale: The preperitoneal approach can inspect and cover both inguinal and femoral openings, addressing the unresolved compartment in this nonpregnant woman.
choices.temptation: Use sex-specific missed-femoral risk and actual scan coverage to choose the offered approach.
choices.counterfactual: Major prior pelvic surgery or a requirement for local anesthesia would change the balance and require tailored planning.

choices.label: Open anterior Shouldice tissue repair
choices.rationale: An anterior tissue repair does not resolve the unassessed femoral compartment; no non-mesh preference supplies a reason to favor it here.
choices.temptation: Choose a primary inguinal tissue repair without resolving broader groin coverage.
choices.counterfactual: A selected primary unilateral inguinal hernia after femoral disease is excluded and informed non-mesh choice could support expert Shouldice repair.

nodes.explanation: The scan characterizes an inguinal finding but not the whole groin. In nonpregnant women, a laparo-endoscopic preperitoneal approach helps avoid missed femoral disease and covers both openings. TAPP is the offered posterior option; this question does not claim superiority over TEP or make laparoscopy mandatory despite a genuine contraindication.

gate.interpret: Interpret the acquisition boundary and clinical fullness as incomplete characterization rather than proof of isolated inguinal disease.
gate.apply: Apply the female groin repair-coverage consideration to the offered operations and actual eligibility.
gate.cueAttack: The task avoids saying comprehensive coverage, and no option alone contains a combined inguinal/femoral phrase. The general-anesthesia and pelvic-history constraints are necessary for this operative comparison and apply to the full option set.
gate.stageCategory: Elective operation selection, three actual repairs.
gate.difficulty: Predicted moderate: a plausible inguinal scan label and common anterior repair compete with the unassessed female femoral compartment.
gate.decidingObservation: The acquisition stops at the ligament while the clinical fullness crosses the crease in a nonpregnant woman.
gate.counterfactual: Add major pelvic dissection or a need for local anesthesia: a routine posterior preference becomes less secure and anterior planning may be favored.
gate.deletionTest: Sex, acquisition coverage, symptom burden and operative constraints determine the approach; none is an epidemiological selection weight.
gate.sequenceCheck: Standalone; no prior classification answer supplies a femoral diagnosis.

nodes.identityReason: New hospital reduction-selection construct; distinct from the old clinic transfer safety identity.
nodes.objective: Separate acute irreducibility from suspected tissue ischemia when considering an initial monitored reduction attempt.
nodes.currentUpdate: The outside emergency surgical service reports that Noah's previously reducing inguinal lump has remained out since a lifting episode. He has localized discomfort without increasing continuous pain. The overlying skin has its usual color, the abdomen is soft without guarding, and he has no vomiting or systemic deterioration. Monitored analgesia and surgical rescue are part of that service's care.
nodes.stem: Which initial hernia-directed intervention should be recommended for Noah's hospital episode?

choices.label: Proceed directly to operative groin exploration
choices.rationale: Operation becomes necessary after failed reduction or suspected ischemia. The represented low-ischemia-concern acute episode can first be considered for gentle reduction.
choices.temptation: Equate acute irreducibility with proven strangulation.
choices.counterfactual: Increasing continuous pain, discolored skin, guarding or failed gentle reduction would favor operative exploration.

choices.label: Attempt gentle monitored manual reduction
choices.rationale: A previously reducing hernia has become acutely irreducible without suspected bowel ischemia. Current guidance supports considering gentle reduction in this hospital setting.
choices.temptation: Use the clinical ischemia assessment rather than the label irreducible alone.
choices.counterfactual: If bowel compromise were suspected, reduction would give way to emergency operative assessment.

choices.label: Defer intervention for overnight reassessment
choices.rationale: An acutely irreducible hernia needs urgent surgical attention. Monitoring is part of active assessment, not a substitute for addressing irreducibility.
choices.temptation: Treat stable circulation as permission to leave an acute fixed hernia unresolved.
choices.counterfactual: A long-standing unchanged irreducible lump without new symptoms would represent a different nonacute pathway.

nodes.explanation: Acute irreducibility and strangulation are different findings. A gentle monitored reduction attempt is supported when the hospital team has no ischemia concern; failed reduction or new concern requires emergency surgery. No forceful office reduction, medication dose or fixed time window is authorized by this draft.

gate.interpret: Use the change from prior reducibility plus the current observed pain, skin and abdominal findings to characterize the episode.
gate.apply: Choose an urgent reduction attempt rather than compulsory immediate surgery or passive delay.
gate.cueAttack: The skin, abdominal and pain observations preserve reduction safety without supplying an ischemia interpretation; the learner distinguishes irreducibility from strangulation. Options are specific interventions at the same immediate phase.
gate.stageCategory: Initial hospital hernia intervention, reviewed in clinic.
gate.difficulty: Predicted moderate, with a safety component: overcalling strangulation and delaying stable patients are competing errors. Difficulty remains qualitative and the weak evidence is explicit.
gate.decidingObservation: Recent loss of reducibility without a concerning clinical ischemia pattern.
gate.counterfactual: Add progressive continuous pain and skin discoloration, or a failed attempt: operative exploration becomes preferred.
gate.deletionTest: Removing the acute change conflates chronic irreducibility; removing ischemia assessment makes the reduction key unsafe.
gate.sequenceCheck: Standalone hospital chart review; a simple sedation-recovery follow-up was removed after the author gate because it did not predict resident-level difficulty.

nodes.identityReason: New operative viability-assessment construct after the sac contents reduce before inspection.
nodes.objective: Recognize that disappearance of a concerning hernia does not establish bowel viability.
nodes.currentUpdate: Iris's outside hospital record describes a tender fixed femoral lump with diminished enhancement of trapped bowel on contrast CT. The surgical team had begun emergency repair. After induction the lump disappeared before the bowel could be inspected. She is hemodynamically stable, and the operative team has laparoscopic expertise.
nodes.stem: Which operative step should the hospital team take next in Iris's recorded operation?

choices.label: Inspect the reduced bowel laparoscopically
choices.rationale: The previously concerning bowel has not been assessed. Diagnostic laparoscopy can inspect viability after spontaneous reduction in this stable setting.
choices.temptation: Separate disappearance of the lump from evidence about the previously trapped tissue.
choices.counterfactual: If the bowel had already been directly inspected and found viable, that inspection would not need to be repeated solely because a lump had reduced.

choices.label: Complete groin repair and wound closure
choices.rationale: Repairing the defect does not resolve the unassessed viability of bowel that reduced after concerning preoperative findings.
choices.temptation: Use spontaneous reduction as proof that ischemia has reversed.
choices.counterfactual: Directly assessed viable bowel with no residual concern would permit completing the repair.

choices.label: Resect the previously trapped bowel segment
choices.rationale: CT concern establishes a need to assess viability, not irreversible necrosis of an identified segment. No bowel has yet been inspected or located for resection.
choices.temptation: Convert reduced enhancement into proof that resection is required.
choices.counterfactual: Directly visualized irreversibly nonviable bowel would support resection.

nodes.explanation: A vanished lump is not a viability examination. Diagnostic laparoscopy is a supported way to inspect previously concerning bowel after spontaneous reduction in a stable patient with the required expertise. Resection depends on what is found, not on CT concern alone.

gate.interpret: Preserve the earlier ischemia concern despite the new absence of the external lump.
gate.apply: Select direct assessment before either completing repair or committing to resection.
gate.cueAttack: Removed safe/available-laparoscopy praise; operator expertise and stable circulation are genuine feasibility constraints. All options are operative steps, not imaging versus unrelated outpatient care.
gate.stageCategory: Next intraoperative step, outside records reviewed in clinic.
gate.difficulty: Predicted moderate: spontaneous reduction falsely reassures, whereas prior CT can tempt unjustified resection.
gate.decidingObservation: Concerning bowel reduced before inspection, so viability remains unassessed.
gate.counterfactual: Supply direct observation of irreversible necrosis: resection becomes the next step. Supply already documented viable tissue: completing repair becomes reasonable.
gate.deletionTest: Both the earlier compromise and the unperformed inspection are necessary; this is actual chronology, not a missing exported image.
gate.sequenceCheck: Standalone; no prior explanation teaches post-reduction viability assessment.

nodes.identityReason: New groin repair-material eligibility after bowel resection; distinct from the urgency construct.
nodes.objective: Distinguish controlled bowel resection from gross enteric contamination before excluding permanent mesh.
nodes.currentUpdate: At the next clinic chart review, Andre's operative record documents removal of the nonviable trapped bowel and a closed anastomosis. The resection was controlled without enteric spillage. The surgeon reports no perforation, pus or peritonitis, and stable circulation. The remaining decision in the record is how to reinforce the groin defect.
nodes.stem: Which repair policy is supported by Andre's recorded operative field?

choices.label: Defer groin reinforcement to a later operation
choices.rationale: Controlled resection without gross contamination does not require a routine staged groin repair.
choices.temptation: Treat any intestinal procedure as incompatible with definitive hernia repair.
choices.counterfactual: Severe instability or an uncontrolled contaminated field could require a staged strategy.

choices.label: Allow permanent macroporous synthetic mesh repair
choices.rationale: A controlled clean-contaminated resection is not an automatic exclusion of macroporous permanent synthetic mesh. This is eligibility, not a claim that every patient must receive it.
choices.temptation: Classify the actual contamination rather than using resection as a surrogate.
choices.counterfactual: Gross enteric spillage with a small closable defect would change the preferred policy toward tissue repair.

choices.label: Restrict groin reinforcement to primary tissue repair
choices.rationale: Tissue repair remains possible, but excluding permanent mesh solely because bowel was resected is unsupported in the represented controlled field.
choices.temptation: Overgeneralize a contaminated-field restriction to all bowel resections.
choices.counterfactual: Gross contamination with a small defect suitable for direct closure supports a primary tissue strategy.

nodes.explanation: The relevant boundary is the actual operative field, not bowel resection as a binary label. Current HerniaSurge guidance allows macroporous mesh after a controlled clean-contaminated resection; older WSES guidance supports the same eligibility. This weak-evidence comparison does not mandate one material or extend to gross spillage.

gate.interpret: Classify controlled resection without spillage as a different field from enteric contamination.
gate.apply: Decide whether permanent mesh must be excluded, without inventing universal operative superiority.
gate.cueAttack: Repaired an initial material-versus-material ambiguity by asking an eligibility policy. All labels are actual repair policies, without rationale text. The key does not say safe, best or no infection risk.
gate.stageCategory: Definitive groin reinforcement policy after completed source management.
gate.difficulty: Predicted moderate to hard: bowel resection often prompts blanket mesh avoidance, while the field changes that boundary.
gate.decidingObservation: Controlled resection with no spillage, perforation, pus or peritonitis.
gate.counterfactual: Add gross stool spillage and a small closable defect: primary tissue repair becomes the supported policy.
gate.deletionTest: Deleting the field observations leaves only bowel resection and makes mesh eligibility underdetermined.
gate.sequenceCheck: Earlier acute feedback discusses viability and urgency, not wound class or repair material. This later operative record earns a distinct inference.

nodes.identityReason: New gross-contamination and defect-closure decision; not a minor wording variant of controlled resection eligibility.
nodes.objective: Integrate gross enteric spillage and a directly closable small defect to select the offered repair.
nodes.currentUpdate: Lena's outside operative record describes a perforated bowel segment within a femoral sac. Enteric contents spilled into the field before resection. Source control and lavage are complete, circulation is stable, and the groin defect measures 2 cm. The surgeon can approximate its edges without tension.
nodes.stem: Which groin repair should be recommended for Lena's recorded operative field?

choices.label: Permanent macroporous synthetic mesh repair
choices.rationale: The permissive controlled-resection evidence cannot be carried over to gross contamination in a small directly closable defect.
choices.temptation: Ignore the field difference because bowel resection can sometimes accompany mesh repair.
choices.counterfactual: Controlled resection without spillage would permit considering permanent macroporous mesh.

choices.label: Biologic mesh reinforcement of the defect
choices.rationale: The cited older guideline reserves consideration of biologic material for contaminated defects where primary suture is not feasible; direct closure is feasible here.
choices.temptation: Assume contamination automatically requires biologic material.
choices.counterfactual: A defect that cannot be closed directly would require a different specialist reconstruction comparison; biologic material is one weak-evidence option.

choices.label: Primary tissue closure of the groin defect
choices.rationale: For a stable patient with gross contamination and a small directly closable defect, WSES supports primary repair. This is a low-certainty, specifically scoped application.
choices.temptation: Use both actual contamination and closure feasibility.
choices.counterfactual: If the field were controlled without spillage, permanent mesh would become a permissible option rather than being excluded.

nodes.explanation: Gross spillage separates this case from controlled clean-contaminated bowel resection. WSES supports primary tissue repair when such a defect is small and directly closable. Its less-than-3-cm boundary directly supports this constructed 2-cm observation; the recommendation is older and low certainty, not a rule for all contaminated abdominal-wall defects.

gate.interpret: Distinguish actual enteric spillage from resection without contamination, then assess direct closure feasibility.
gate.apply: Choose tissue repair for the represented small closable contaminated defect.
gate.cueAttack: Three parallel repair options, no uniquely cautious combined plan. The exact constructed dimension is directly inside the sourced boundary; it is not a new invented cutoff.
gate.stageCategory: Definitive groin repair after source control, all choices are repairs.
gate.difficulty: Predicted moderate: both permanent-mesh overextension and automatic biologic-mesh substitution are credible errors.
gate.decidingObservation: Gross spillage plus a 2-cm defect whose edges approximate without tension.
gate.counterfactual: Change to controlled resection without spillage: synthetic mesh becomes permissible. Make closure infeasible: the present single primary-closure key loses its support.
gate.deletionTest: Removing contamination or feasibility produces multiple plausible repair strategies.
gate.sequenceCheck: Standalone companion scenario; do not precede it with feedback that states the contamination contrast verbatim. No assembled same-patient sequence is proposed.

nodes.identityReason: New readiness for invasive chronic-pain treatment, distinct from block interpretation or nerve localization.
nodes.objective: Distinguish elapsed time since repair from an adequate trial of structured chronic-pain treatment.
nodes.currentUpdate: At later review, Mara is eight months after open repair. Her wound is healed, repeated targeted examination has not demonstrated recurrence, and pain still limits work. She entered a specialist hernia/pain program two weeks ago, with medication adjustment and injection therapy. She asks for an operation because so much time has passed since repair. No intolerable treatment adverse effect or progressive focal deficit is recorded.
nodes.stem: Which treatment plan should be recommended for Mara at this later review?

choices.label: Proceed to open triple neurectomy
choices.rationale: Passing a postoperative interval is not the same as completing the recommended period of less invasive pain treatment. The available record does not select triple neurectomy now.
choices.temptation: Use the date of the original repair as the sole escalation criterion.
choices.counterfactual: Persistent carefully characterized pain after an adequate specialist treatment course may warrant discussion of tailored surgery, without automatically selecting triple neurectomy.

choices.label: Continue the specialist nonoperative pain program
choices.rationale: The structured trial has just begun. HerniaSurge suggests continuing pharmacologic/interventional measures for at least three months and being at least six months from repair before invasive treatment planning.
choices.temptation: Interpret treatment exposure as well as time since repair.
choices.counterfactual: Persistent disabling pain after a completed adequate treatment course would justify a new multidisciplinary discussion of invasive options.

choices.label: Proceed to anterior mesh explantation
choices.rationale: The record supplies neither a specific mesh complication requiring removal nor an adequate completed conservative course. Mesh removal is not selected by postoperative duration alone.
choices.temptation: Attribute all chronic postrepair pain to implanted material.
choices.counterfactual: A documented mesh-related complication after adequate evaluation may support tailored expert surgery, with its risks considered.

nodes.explanation: Mara has passed the postoperative interval but has only begun structured pain treatment. Continue the specialist pharmacologic/interventional program and reassess. The guideline's minimum intervals do not establish that surgery becomes mandatory after they pass, and any future operation requires individualized evidence and counseling about failure or worsened pain.

gate.interpret: Distinguish eight months since repair from two weeks in the actual structured treatment program.
gate.apply: Apply readiness for invasive escalation, retaining specialist care rather than selecting a fixed operation.
gate.cueAttack: The previous partial block response is not reinterpreted as a surgical indication. Three concrete treatment policies at the same decision phase; exact clinical intervals are sourced, not diagnostic wait durations.
gate.stageCategory: Escalation of chronic postoperative pain treatment after recurrence assessment.
gate.difficulty: Predicted moderate: elapsed postoperative time and prior partial block response tempt premature surgery.
gate.decidingObservation: The pain program has lasted two weeks despite eight months since repair.
gate.counterfactual: Supply an adequate completed specialist treatment course with persistent disabling symptoms: reconsider invasive planning; the exact operation still requires new evidence.
gate.deletionTest: Deleting either interval hides the tested distinction. The lack of progressive deficit/urgent complication preserves a fair conservative-versus-invasive comparison.
gate.sequenceCheck: Prior feedback limits block localization and does not supply the later treatment interval. The new treatment-exposure record is essential to this node.

nodes.identityReason: New postrepair pain-site/provenance decision, distinct from a named cutaneous nerve-localization question.
nodes.objective: Distinguish pain in scrotal contents from mapped scrotal-skin symptoms before selecting the diagnostic referral.
nodes.currentUpdate: Rafael describes an ongoing ache within the right testicle after open inguinal repair. Pinprick and light touch over the groin and scrotal skin are symmetric and do not reproduce it. Gentle palpation of the testicle reproduces his usual ache. The groin scar is healed, and dynamic groin examination shows no impulse. There has been no sudden severe onset or systemic illness.
nodes.stem: Which evaluation should next address Rafael's postrepair pain?

choices.label: Genital-branch block with cutaneous mapping
choices.rationale: A skin nerve target is not established by pain reproduced within the testicle while the skin examination is unremarkable.
choices.temptation: Treat scrotal skin innervation as the explanation for all scrotal-content pain.
choices.counterfactual: Mapped scrotal-skin burning/allodynia could support a targeted specialist cutaneous nerve evaluation.

choices.label: Urological assessment of the scrotal contents
choices.rationale: True testicular pain requires assessment of the contents and relevant urological causes; it should not be assumed to be cutaneous postherniorrhaphy neuropathy.
choices.temptation: Preserve the tissue/site distinction before selecting a nerve procedure.
choices.counterfactual: If light touch over mapped scrotal skin reproduced the symptom and contents were painless, a cutaneous pain pathway would be more appropriate.

choices.label: Hernia-surgery assessment for mesh removal
choices.rationale: The current record does not establish mesh as the source. Evaluate the symptomatic contents before selecting a mesh-directed intervention.
choices.temptation: Use the temporal association with repair to infer a specific mesh complication.
choices.counterfactual: A demonstrated mesh-related complication after specialist workup could justify tailored surgical assessment.

nodes.explanation: Rafael's symptom is reproduced in the testicular contents rather than the scrotal skin. HerniaSurge distinguishes those sources and supports formal urological evaluation for orchialgia. A prior hernia operation does not establish that a cutaneous nerve block or mesh removal addresses this pain.

gate.interpret: Localize the reproduced symptom to contents rather than scrotal skin using the actual examination.
gate.apply: Choose urological assessment instead of a cutaneous block or presumed mesh surgery.
gate.cueAttack: No orchialgia or genitofemoral diagnosis is supplied before the task. All choices are specific diagnostic/specialist pathways, with the block's wait mapped. Sudden onset is excluded because it would change urgency.
gate.stageCategory: Next diagnostic evaluation of persistent postrepair pain.
gate.difficulty: Predicted moderate: using the genital branch for every scrotal symptom is a credible surgical error.
gate.decidingObservation: Testicular palpation reproduces the usual ache while skin stimulation does not.
gate.counterfactual: Move the reproduced pain to a mapped skin distribution with painless contents: targeted cutaneous nerve evaluation becomes reasonable.
gate.deletionTest: Deleting tissue-specific examination collapses the distinction. The nonacute course prevents a hidden acute-scrotum emergency.
gate.sequenceCheck: Standalone; no prior nerve-localization answer supplies the referral.

nodes.identityReason: New anesthesia/repair-context decision within the groin topic; no generic anesthetic-drug objective.
nodes.objective: Choose anesthesia for an experienced team's open reducible inguinal repair in a frail older adult.
nodes.currentUpdate: Evan has a unilateral reducing inguinal hernia that interrupts dressing and walking. He has severe chronic pulmonary disease without a current exacerbation and previously needed catheterization after spinal anesthesia. The team plans an open Lichtenstein repair. He can cooperate during the procedure, and the team routinely uses both local and general techniques for this operation.
nodes.stem: Which anesthetic approach should be favored for Evan's planned open inguinal repair?

choices.label: Spinal anesthesia
choices.rationale: Regional anesthesia is not the favored alternative in this older frail patient with prior retention. Local open repair is an established option with appropriate expertise.
choices.temptation: Assume every way of avoiding general anesthesia has the same risk profile.
choices.counterfactual: A patient-specific anesthetic assessment may sometimes favor regional care; that preference is not established by this record.

choices.label: General anesthesia
choices.rationale: General anesthesia is possible, but the severe pulmonary comorbidity, cooperative patient and experienced local-repair team support favoring local anesthesia here.
choices.temptation: Apply the common laparoscopic anesthetic pathway to an already chosen open operation.
choices.counterfactual: An uncooperative patient or operation not suitable for the team's local technique could favor general anesthesia.

choices.label: Local infiltration anesthesia
choices.rationale: Experienced local anesthesia is recommended for open reducible inguinal repair and is useful in frail/co-morbid patients. It avoids treating spinal anesthesia as an automatically safer substitute.
choices.temptation: Match the operation, comorbidity and actual ability to cooperate to the anesthetic option.
choices.counterfactual: If cooperation were impossible or the repair required a different anesthetic plan, this preference would require reassessment.

nodes.explanation: For an experienced team's open repair of a reducing inguinal hernia, local anesthesia is supported and can benefit frail patients. Evan's pulmonary disease and prior retention make an automatic switch to general or spinal anesthesia less attractive. No drug, dose or universal anesthetic contraindication is authored.

gate.interpret: Use the actual planned open operation and comorbid/previous anesthetic response, rather than a universal laparoscopic preference.
gate.apply: Favor local anesthesia when both cooperation and experienced local technique are represented.
gate.cueAttack: All options are anesthetic techniques, not combined operations. Expertise applies to the comparison and is a genuine prerequisite; the task does not call any option safer by name.
gate.stageCategory: Anesthesia selection for an already selected open groin repair.
gate.difficulty: Predicted moderate: spinal may seem the obvious way to avoid general anesthesia but has a relevant competing risk.
gate.decidingObservation: Frail pulmonary patient, prior spinal-associated retention, cooperative behavior and an experienced local-repair team.
gate.counterfactual: Make cooperation impossible or change the required operation: general anesthesia may be favored after assessment.
gate.deletionTest: Removing the planned operation, cooperation or experience makes local technique unfair; prior retention and pulmonary disease create the specific tradeoff.
gate.sequenceCheck: Standalone; does not change the anesthesia topic's general drug or airway content.

nodes.identityReason: New technique-dependent mesh material objective, distinct from recurrence-plane selection.
nodes.objective: Avoid transferring the open Lichtenstein lightweight-mesh preference to a large direct posterior repair.
nodes.currentUpdate: At later planning review, Nolan's surgeon describes a broad medial defect for the agreed posterior repair. Two equally sized macroporous permanent polypropylene meshes can provide the planned overlap and fixation. One is classified lightweight and the other heavyweight. Nolan's priority is avoiding another recurrence, and he asks whether the lighter implant will also reduce chronic pain in this operation.
nodes.stem: Which mesh should be favored for Nolan's planned posterior repair of the broad direct defect?

choices.label: The lightweight polypropylene mesh
choices.rationale: The chronic-pain advantage described for lightweight material in open Lichtenstein repair does not carry over to posterior repair; recurrence is a concern in large direct defects.
choices.temptation: Generalize a material preference across different operative techniques.
choices.counterfactual: For an open Lichtenstein repair, lightweight mesh is guideline-supported for pain/foreign-body outcomes.

choices.label: The heavyweight polypropylene mesh
choices.rationale: HerniaSurge recommends heavier mesh in laparo-endoscopic repair, particularly large direct defects, to reduce recurrence; lighter mesh has not shown the proposed chronic-pain advantage in that setting.
choices.temptation: Condition the material choice on technique and defect rather than weight in isolation.
choices.counterfactual: Changing to an open anterior Lichtenstein operation changes the guideline's weight preference.

choices.label: Either mesh with no material preference
choices.rationale: Equivalent size and planned fixation do not establish equivalent recurrence behavior for a broad direct posterior defect in the guideline comparison.
choices.temptation: Assume similar coverage cancels technique-specific material evidence.
choices.counterfactual: For a small lateral posterior defect, the recurrence-weight difference is less supported and a categorical heavy preference is less secure.

nodes.explanation: Mesh weight is not a technique-independent rule. The posterior large-direct setting supports heavier material for recurrence prevention, whereas lightweight mesh is favored in open Lichtenstein repair for pain/foreign-body outcomes. This draft specifies no new numerical weight or defect-size cutoff and makes no all-patient pain guarantee.

gate.interpret: Combine the posterior technique with the broad medial defect rather than treating lighter mesh as universally better.
gate.apply: Apply the technique-specific weight recommendation to the patient's recurrence priority.
gate.cueAttack: Mesh size, composition, overlap and fixation are common so the key is not uniquely complete. Labels have comparable specificity. The equivocal option is an actual material policy, not a vague individualized answer.
gate.stageCategory: Mesh selection after repair approach is settled.
gate.difficulty: Predicted moderate to hard: importing an open-repair pain preference into posterior repair is the central error.
gate.decidingObservation: Broad direct defect treated posteriorly, with both meshes otherwise suitable for the planned repair.
gate.counterfactual: Change the operation to open Lichtenstein: the lightweight choice becomes preferred for the guideline's pain/foreign-body outcomes.
gate.deletionTest: Removing technique or defect type makes the weight preference poorly specified; exact grams are unnecessary and omitted.
gate.sequenceCheck: The earlier plane answer does not mention material weight or chronic-pain evidence. This later technical planning record supplies a distinct decision.

nodes.identityReason: New adult pregnancy exception and vascular mimic; childhood groin decisions remain outside this lane.
nodes.objective: Interpret vascular groin findings during pregnancy before applying the nonpregnant-woman hernia-repair rule.
nodes.currentUpdate: Aisha is pregnant and has painless right groin fullness that increases while standing and empties supine. Color Doppler shows compressible serpiginous channels along the round ligament with venous flow augmented during strain. Repeated dynamic views show no protruding bowel or fat sac. She has no acute pain, erythema or vomiting.
nodes.stem: Which groin plan should be recommended for Aisha at this clinic review?

choices.label: Arrange elective preperitoneal hernia repair during pregnancy
choices.rationale: The record describes a vascular mimic rather than an established visceral hernia. The nonpregnant female hernia policy cannot be applied indiscriminately.
choices.temptation: Treat female groin swelling as a repair indication without interpreting Doppler.
choices.counterfactual: A true complicated hernia with threatened contents would require surgical assessment regardless of pregnancy.

choices.label: Arrange operative excision of the inguinal swelling
choices.rationale: Uncomplicated round-ligament venous enlargement during pregnancy commonly supports observation rather than excision.
choices.temptation: Treat a reducible-appearing vascular swelling as a mass requiring removal.
choices.counterfactual: Severe persistent symptoms or a complication would prompt specialist reassessment rather than routine observation.

choices.label: Observe the groin swelling with return precautions
choices.rationale: Venous channels along the round ligament without a visceral sac support a pregnancy-associated vascular mimic and expectant care in this uncomplicated course.
choices.temptation: Interpret the channels and flow before importing a hernia management rule.
choices.counterfactual: New severe pain, inflammatory change or a bowel-containing fixed sac would require urgent reassessment.

nodes.explanation: The observed venous channels support round-ligament varicosities, not a demonstrated bowel/fat hernia sac. Uncomplicated pregnancy-associated swelling can be observed with reassessment for new symptoms. The supporting literature is small-cohort/case-series evidence and does not justify ignoring a painful or compromised groin finding.

gate.interpret: Interpret compressible venous channels rather than assuming the reducing contour is a visceral hernia.
gate.apply: Apply the pregnancy/mimic boundary before choosing observation versus operative treatment.
gate.cueAttack: Removed varicosity and hernia labels from the pre-answer context. Three concrete management options; Doppler is an observed acquired result with no invented diagnostic cutoff.
gate.stageCategory: Management of an acquired vascular groin finding during pregnancy.
gate.difficulty: Predicted moderate: a generic female-groin repair rule competes with the specific Doppler and pregnancy evidence.
gate.decidingObservation: Venous-flow channels along the round ligament with no dynamically demonstrated visceral sac and no acute symptoms.
gate.counterfactual: Replace channels with a fixed bowel-containing sac and ischemic concern: urgent operative assessment replaces observation.
gate.deletionTest: Removing Doppler or pregnancy eliminates the reason not to apply the standard nonpregnant repair discussion.
gate.sequenceCheck: Standalone; not immediately preceded by the nonpregnant-woman repair explanation.
